kernels.l1: One hoop shared out across two others gives the same shading either way.
kernels.l2: When you overlap one hoop with two hoops joined together, you can do it one hoop at a time and join the answers. The shading comes out the same.
kernels.l3: Intersecting with a union can be done piece by piece: S ∩ (T ∪ R) is the same as (S ∩ T) ∪ (S ∩ R). Unlike arithmetic, the reverse also works — union spreads across intersection too.
kernels.l4: S ∩ (T ∪ R) = (S∩T) ∪ (S∩R) and S ∪ (T∩R) = (S∪T) ∩ (S∪R). Unlike arithmetic, where only × distributes over +, both set operations distribute over each other.
kernels.l5: Both distributive laws hold for sets, each proved by double inclusion with a case split in one direction; the symmetry has no arithmetic analogue.
kernels.l6: ∩ and ∪ distribute over each other, making P(X) a distributive lattice — a property arithmetic lacks and Boolean algebra requires.
kernels.l7: Intersection distributes over union and union distributes over intersection; the two laws are De Morgan duals, and their symmetry distinguishes the lattice P(X) from the arithmetic of + and ×.
kernels.l8: Mutual distributivity makes P(X) a distributive lattice; failure of one law characterises non-distributive lattices such as the subspace lattice of a vector space, which is where quantum logic departs from classical.
